query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Doping the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a small trace amount of yttrium will promote the in situ formation of a stable, adherent, and lubricious oxide scale that maintains low friction and wear across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix in its standard, unmodified composition
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor yttrium doping (via the addition of a rare‐earth element) into the alloy composition
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in air performed over a temperature range from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C under controlled normal loads (e.g., ~5–10 N) typical of tribological evaluations
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, stable oxide layer with yttrium segregation at grain boundaries which enhances oxide adhesion and integrity
generation.mechanism: The yttrium doping is expected to modify the oxidation kinetics such that a protective, self-lubricating oxide glaze forms. This layer resists spallation and maintains cohesive bonding under both low and high temperature sliding conditions, thereby reducing friction and wear compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi material, the yttrium-doped alloy should exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced specific wear rate throughout the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which suffers from unstable oxide layer formation and increased wear and friction at elevated temperatures
generation.boundary: Temperature range: ~25 °C to 800 °C; environmental condition: air; applied load: ~5–10 N during sliding wear tests
generation.uncertainty: The exact yttrium concentration required for optimal oxide scale formation and the quantitative improvement in tribological properties could vary depending on processing conditions and may require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one set doped with a small percentage of yttrium. Perform identical sliding wear tests in air at set temperature intervals from room temperature to 800 °C under a constant normal load (~5–10 N) using the same reciprocating tribometer. Characterize the tribological performance by measuring the friction coefficient, specific wear rate, and the morphology and adherence of the oxide scale using SEM/EDS and XRD.
measurements: Real-time coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Wear volume to calculate specific wear rate
Microscopic analysis of the oxide scale structure and adherence (via SEM/EDS, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the entire temperature range compared to the baseline alloy, or if the oxide scale shows no improvement in adhesion or stability, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

cited_evidence.kind: web:2.1. Experimental Equipment and Sample Preparation
cited_evidence.text: An LDM diode laser system from Germany’s Laserline was employed (Mülheim-Kärlich, Germany), with a laser power of 3000 W, a scanning speed of 4 mm/s, and an overlap rate of 50%. The schematic diagram of the equipment is shown in Figure 1. The cladding materials used were Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 high-entropy alloy powder prepared by vacuum atomization and high-purity Y2O3 rare earth oxide powder. The average particle size of the Y2O3 rare earth oxide was 10 μm. The Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 alloy powder had a particle size range of 53–150 μm and a chemical composition of 6.05% Al, 20.34% Nb, 10.90% Ti, 11.16% V, and the balance Ni (wt.%). The mixed powder was placed in a ball mill together with stainless steel balls of 5 mm diameter and subjected to ball milling at a rotation speed of 30 r/min for 20 min. Four Ni50(AlNbTiV)50-xY2O3 (x = 0 wt.%, 0.2 wt.%, 0.4 wt.%, and 0.6 wt.%) composite coatings were prepared, denoted as Y0, Y1, Y2, and Y3, respectively.

frame.system: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix in its standard (unmodified) composition as used in sliding wear tests
frame.goal: Achieve a consistently low coefficient of friction and minimized wear rate across the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C
frame.limitation: The baseline CoCrFeNi HEA shows difficulty in maintaining low friction and wear resistance over a wide temperature window, likely due to temperature‐dependent degradation mechanisms such as oxide scale formation and spallation.
root_cause_cues: wear rate throughout the full temperature range
constraints: load and environmental conditions typical for sliding in air
frame.regime: Sliding wear tests conducted in air over a temperature range from ~25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C under controlled load conditions representative of practical applications
prior_attempts: Unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy performance showing degraded friction and wear at high temperatures
Implicit prior experiments that failed to achieve a uniform lubrication mechanism across the full temperature span
frame.understanding: Introducing a minor trace doping of a rare-earth element (e.g., yttrium) into the CoCrFeNi matrix is hypothesized to promote the in situ formation of a stable, adherent, and lubricious oxide scale. Yttrium is expected to segregate to oxide grain boundaries during high-temperature sliding, thereby suppressing spallation and enhancing oxide scale cohesion. This mechanism should maintain low friction and wear from room temperature through 800 °C. Prior evidence from Ni-based superalloys shows that rare-earth additions improve high-temperature oxidation resistance and tribological performance. A controlled falsification experiment would compare tribological performance between the base alloy and yttrium-doped samples under identical sliding conditions with defined loads and temperatures, analyzing friction coefficients, wear rates, and oxide scale morphology to confirm the efficacy of the yttrium intervention.
